quiz.q: What does `.map()` do when added to a lazy iterator chain?
options: Immediately runs and returns a Vec
Describes a transformation of each item; still does nothing until consumed
Filters out items that fail a test
quiz.explain: Like all adaptors, `.map()` just adds a step to the plan. Nothing runs until a consumer like `.collect()` or a `for` loop pulls values through.

options: filter keeps items passing a test; filter_map both filters and transforms in one step, dropping Nones
quiz.explain: filter_map's closure returns Option<T>: Some(value) keeps the transformed value, None drops the item — one adaptor instead of map + filter + unwrap.

quiz.q: What happens when you `.zip()` two iterators of different lengths?
options: The result has the length of the longer iterator, padding the shorter with None
The result stops as soon as the shorter iterator is exhausted
quiz.explain: zip pairs items positionally and stops the moment either side runs out, so the output length equals the shorter of the two iterators.

quiz.q: Which method pairs each item with its index, starting at 0?
quiz.explain: enumerate() turns an iterator of Item into an iterator of (usize, Item) pairs, with the index starting at 0.

quiz.q: What does `.collect::<Vec<i32>>()` do that a bare `.collect()` sometimes can't?
options: Tells the compiler what type to build, avoiding a 'type annotations needed' error
Makes the chain run eagerly instead of lazily
quiz.explain: collect() can build many different collections, so the compiler needs to know which one. Turbofish (or a type annotation on the binding) supplies that.

quiz.q: What does `nums.iter().fold(0, |acc, n| acc + n)` compute for `[1, 2, 3]`?
quiz.explain: fold carries an accumulator through every item, starting at 0: 0+1=1, 1+2=3, 3+3=6. The final accumulator, 6, is returned.

quiz.q: Why might a plain for loop be preferred over a 6-step adaptor chain?
options: Long chains can become harder to read and debug than a commented for loop
Adaptors don't work with more than 3 steps
for loops don't need a mut binding
quiz.explain: Adaptors are great for straightforward transform/filter/collect work, but a very long chain — or one with side effects — often reads worse than a for loop you can step through line by line.

quiz.q: What does `.take(3)` do to an iterator?
options: Removes the first 3 items and returns the rest
Yields only the first 3 items, ignoring the rest
Takes ownership of only the first 3 items
quiz.explain: take(n) limits the stream to at most the first n items; everything after is never yielded.

options: sum() adds up numeric items; count() tells you how many items came through, regardless of value
sum() returns an Option, count() returns a Result
quiz.explain: sum() totals the numeric values in the iterator. count() ignores the values entirely and just tallies how many items were produced.

flashcards.front: What do adaptors like map, filter, and enumerate have in common?
flashcards.back: They're all lazy — each describes a step in the pipeline but runs no code until a consumer pulls values through.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between filter and filter_map?
flashcards.back: filter keeps items where a closure returns true. filter_map runs a closure returning Option<T> per item — Some is kept and unwrapped, None is dropped. One step instead of filter + map + unwrap.

flashcards.front: How long does .zip() run when the two iterators have different lengths?
flashcards.back: It stops as soon as either iterator runs out — the result length is the shorter of the two.

flashcards.front: How do you tell .collect() what type to build?
flashcards.back: Either a type annotation on the binding (`let v: Vec<i32> = ...`) or turbofish syntax (`.collect::<Vec<i32>>()`).
Builds up a single accumulated value by applying the closure to each item in turn, starting from init. sum() is really a specialized fold.

flashcards.front: When does a for loop read better than an adaptor chain?
flashcards.back: When the chain gets long (roughly 4-5+ adaptors), has side effects like I/O, or needs intermediate debugging — a commented for loop is often clearer.

flashcards.front: What does enumerate() add to each item?
flashcards.back: Its index, yielding (usize, Item) pairs starting at 0.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between sum() and count()?
flashcards.back: sum() adds up the numeric values of items into a total. count() just tallies how many items passed through, regardless of their value.
